text: Rust allows only one mutable reference to a value at a time so that a write is exclusive: nothing else can read or write that memory while the reference exists. That rule prevents data races, where two or more accesses touch the same data at once, at least one of them writes, and there is no synchronization.
thought:
The user is asking a conceptual question about Rust's borrow checker.

Rust enforces aliasing rules that permit either one mutable reference or any number of shared references to the same value, but never both. This prevents data races.

It also prevents iterator invalidation and use-after-free bugs. Aliasing mutable references would allow undefined behavior from simultaneous mutation.

The Rust borrow checker treats `&mut T` as unique. Two mutable references to the same value would let one mutation invalidate the other's assumptions. This prevents double-free and similar memory-safety bugs even in single-threaded code.

The Rust Book frames this as preventing data races. Data races require concurrent unsynchronized access, so the compile error also blocks aliasing bugs in single-threaded code.
